The original Norwegian title, Drømmer, hovers between nocturnal vision and aspiration, between fantasy and the longing to be read — leaving one to ask: when a feeling becomes a text, to whom does it then belong? For admirers of the contemporary Scandinavian conversation film and the literary chamber drama, Dreams advances the form by making the act of reading aloud itself the central cinematic event.

Hong Sang-soo (b. 1960), South Korea's preeminent miniaturist of soju-soaked talk and structural rhyme, makes in Like You Know It All a self-reflexive entry in an oeuvre already devoted, since The Day a Pig Fell into the Well (1996), to the gulf between how people narrate themselves and how they behave; his trademark zooms, doubled episodes, and quotidian humiliations here turn the lens squarely on his own profession. The film converges two charged Korean spaces—the inland festival town of Jecheon and the volcanic resort of Jeju Island—into a single psychological terrain where provincial earnestness and holiday self-delusion mirror one another. Its protagonist, the art-house director Ku Kyeong-nam, arrives as the familiar Hongian figure of the cultured man-of-letters, only to subvert that archetype into something closer to a fraud caught mid-performance. The title's needling phrase—the implication that one acts as though one understands everything—resolves into a Hwadu: can anyone truly know another, or even oneself? For admirers of the festival-circuit auteur film and the loose Korean New Wave inheritance after Im Kwon-taek, this is Hong refining his comedy of self-knowledge into its most pitilessly funny and structurally elegant form.

Anthony Russo (b. 1970), who with his brother Joe migrated from the sitcom rhythms of Arrested Development and Community into Marvel's blockbuster machine, brings to this thirteenth Marvel Cinematic Universe entry a procedural restraint that distinguishes it from the genre's usual operatic excess—a sensibility honed on their preceding The Winter Soldier, which reframed the superhero film as paranoid 1970s political thriller. The film's geography is itself an argument: a Berlin facility where flags and treaties convene, and a derelict Siberian bunker frozen in Cold War rot, two poles between which the bright multinational fiction of the Avengers dissolves into private grief. Its center is Steve Rogers, the New Deal soldier-as-conscience, an Antigone who places loyalty to a single wounded friend above the codified law of nations—and who, in transcending the boy-scout archetype, becomes something stranger and more troubling. The very word 'Civil War' promises a clash of ideologies, yet asks quietly whether any war is ever fought for the reasons its combatants announce: is conviction merely the costume worn by wounds? Advancing the post-Avengers 'shared universe' crossover into the register of tragedy, it tests whether spectacle cinema can bear the weight of irreparable rupture.

Emile Ardolino (b. 1943), a documentarian of dance who won an Oscar for the 1983 PBS profile *He Makes Me Feel Like Dancin'* before turning to fiction, brought a choreographer's literal sense of the body's truth to this, his feature debut. The film converges two American symbolic spaces: the Catskills' fading Borscht Belt resort, those Jewish-vacationer havens of the postwar Northeast, and an after-hours staff quarters that throbs like a Harlem rent party—daylight propriety pressed against nocturnal release. Its protagonist, Frances 'Baby' Houseman, enters as a Cinderella in reverse—a doctor's privileged daughter who must descend rather than ascend to find transformation—then quietly subverts the rescued-ingénue archetype. The very phrase *Dirty Dancing* fuses sex and class shame into one adjective, raising a Hwadu: what exactly is 'dirty,' the dancing or the world that names it so? Released in 1987 from the small Vestron Pictures, this is a coming-of-age musical that, beneath its jukebox sheen and now-canonical numbers, smuggles in the politics of abortion, class, and bodily autonomy on the eve of the Civil Rights summer. It advances the teen-musical romance into something startlingly historical—and worth re-watching with open eyes.

Chris Columbus (b. 1958), the Spielberg-trained architect of family blockbusters from Home Alone (1990) to Mrs. Doubtfire (1993), here assumes the role of faithful translator, building the first cinematic brick of a franchise that would redefine the relationship between literary phenomenon and screen institution. Between a cupboard under the stairs on Privet Drive and the turreted silhouette of Hogwarts rising across a black lake, the film draws a symbolic axis between domestic exile and mythic belonging, between the suburban prison of Surrey and the gothic sanctuary of the boarding-school imagination. Its protagonist, Harry Potter, arrives as a textbook orphan-hero in the lineage of Oliver Twist and Arthur of Camelot, yet his power is curiously passive—a fame he inherits rather than earns. The English title, Philosopher's Stone (Americanized to Sorcerer's Stone), invokes the alchemists' dream of transmutation and eternal life: what does it mean that the most desired object in a children's story is the conquest of death itself? As the founding text of the early-2000s fantasy-adaptation cycle that ran parallel to Peter Jackson's Tolkien, this film advances the genre by proving that the modern multiplex could become a cathedral of childhood myth.

Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi (b. 1979), the Hungarian-American documentarian who co-directs with husband and elite climber Jimmy Chin, arrives here at the summit of a vérité tradition that runs from the Maysles brothers through the adrenaline lyricism of mountain cinema, fusing intimate domestic observation with technically unprecedented vertical photography. The film's symbolic landscape is the meeting of two Yosemite presences—the 3,000-foot granite monolith of El Capitan, sculpted by Pleistocene glaciers and worshipped since Carleton Watkins's 1861 photographs, and the cramped interior of a parked van that becomes its psychic opposite. At its center is Alex Honnold, a free-solo climber who at first resembles the lone Romantic mountaineer in the lineage of Caspar David Friedrich's wanderer, only to subvert that myth with a clinician's affectlessness and a brain scan that reframes courage as neurology. The title 'Free Solo' names a discipline stripped of rope and partner, yet it whispers a Hwadu: when a life is reduced to a single perfect performance with no second chance, is such freedom the highest self-mastery or the loneliest form of bondage? As a landmark of the modern adventure documentary, it advances the form by making the apparatus of witnessing—and its ethical weight—part of the drama itself.

Spike Lee (b. 1957), the restless chronicler of urban America whose joints from Do the Right Thing to Malcolm X fuse expressionist colour, the signature dolly 'double' shot, and a moral fury inherited from the Black New Wave, here turns inward and elegiac. The film maps a New York suspended between two voids: Carraway-glamour and the still-smouldering pit of Ground Zero, the Hudson River pulling westward toward an America of second chances. Its protagonist, Monty Brogan—convicted drug dealer played by Edward Norton—wears the doomed-night-before mask of a condemned Everyman, a Socrates awaiting the hemlock, yet refuses the consolations the archetype offers. The title's '25th hour'—the impossible time beyond the twenty-four, the hour after the deadline when reprieve is no longer possible—frames a single question: when no escape remains, what is the difference between accepting your fate and inventing the life you forfeited? Adapted from David Benioff's pre-9/11 novel and reshot in a city in mourning, 25th Hour stands as the first major American drama to absorb the attacks into its very grain, advancing the post-9/11 urban elegy not through spectacle but through grief, guilt, and the slow grey light of a wounded metropolis.

Oliver Hirschbiegel (b. 1957), a German director schooled in the claustrophobic dread of his 2001 prison-psychology thriller Das Experiment, turns his clinical eye on the most forbidden interior in modern German history. The film converges two spaces into one symbolic crucible: the besieged streets of Berlin above, where the Red Army grinds toward the Reichstag, and the sealed concrete labyrinth of the Führerbunker below, an airless tomb where the air-conditioning hums while a regime suffocates. Its witness is not a general but Traudl Junge, the young secretary whose ordinary loyalty makes her a kind of inverted Virgil, guiding us through an inferno that refuses the comfort of monsters. The German title Der Untergang means not merely a 'downfall' but a sinking, a going-under—a Wagnerian Götterdämmerung emptied of its gods, leaving only flesh, fear, and a trembling hand. What happens to evil when it is filmed at close range, eating, weeping, and dying like any man? Arriving amid a German cinema finally confronting its past head-on—following Das Boot and anticipating The Lives of Others—Downfall advances the historical reconstruction film into the perilous territory of empathy, daring the viewer to look at the abyss without flinching, and without forgiving.

Todd Douglas Miller (b. 1976), an American documentarian schooled in archival recovery rather than talking-head exposition, here perfects a found-footage purism that descends from the direct cinema of the Maysles brothers and the time-image patience of Frederick Wiseman, yet outstrips both by working from rediscovered 70mm large-format reels and unmixed NASA audio. The film stages its drama across two converging spaces: the swamp-flat expanse of Florida's Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral and the abstract, gridded void of Houston's Mission Control, the terrestrial and the cosmic folding into a single nervous system of glass, dust, and signal. At its center stands commander Neil Armstrong — outwardly the laconic test-pilot hero in the lineage of the Mercury Seven, yet so withholding that he subverts the very astronaut-icon he embodies, a face that gives almost nothing back to the lens. The title names a number and a god of light, of prophecy, of distance: what does it mean to call a machine after Apollo and then point it at the silent Moon? Restoring the launch documentary as pure observational spectacle, Apollo 11 advances the archival nonfiction film into a realm where editing alone becomes suspense, history becomes present tense, and the past is screened as if it had never finished happening.

Nitesh Tiwari (b. 1974), the engineer-turned-filmmaker whose work bridges advertising-honed kineticism and the emotionally maximalist tradition of mainstream Hindi cinema, here crafts his most disciplined fusion of sports-biopic rigour and family melodrama. The film maps a symbolic terrain stretching from the dusty akharas of Balali in Haryana — India's wrestling heartland and one of its most patriarchal regions — to the air-conditioned anonymity of the National Sports Academy in Patiala, two poles between which an entire nation's contradictions about its daughters are staged. Its protagonist, the failed-champion-turned-father Mahavir Singh Phogat (Aamir Khan, aging across decades), recalls the archetype of the obsessive paternal Pygmalion — the maker who would sculpt a child into the realization of his own thwarted dream — yet the film complicates whether such love liberates or possesses. The Hindi title 'Dangal' means simply 'wrestling competition,' a folk arena of grappling bodies: but who, ultimately, is wrestling whom — and against what? Advancing the global wave of the inspirational sports biopic while inflecting it with the moral urgency of socially conscious Bollywood, Dangal asks the genre's familiar triumph to carry an unfamiliar weight.

Robert Bresson (b. 1901), the austere French Catholic ascetic whose 'cinematography' purged acting, score, and spectacle in favor of what he called models and the transcendental, here delivers the keystone of a lineage running from Diary of a Country Priest to Mouchette. The action drifts across a sun-flattened French countryside—a hillside farm and the dusty border roads of the Pyrenean foothills—where rural Catholicism's grace and peasant cruelty converge into a single moral terrain. At its center is not a person but Balthazar, a donkey passed hand to hand, an animal protagonist cast in the role of the Holy Fool or suffering saint, yet stripped even of the consolation of self-knowledge that archetype usually grants. The title's invocation of hasard—chance, randomness, the throw of the dice—sits in unbearable tension with the saint's name Balthazar, posing the Hwadu: if a life is governed purely by accident, can suffering still be holy? Emerging at the height of 1966 and the French New Wave's noisier experiments, this film advances the spiritual-minimalist tradition by proving that the deepest interiority can be summoned by withholding expression entirely—and by routing salvation through the eyes of a beast.

Clint Eastwood (b. 1930), the once-iconic gunslinger turned austere elegist of American violence, made this companion to Flags of Our Fathers as the deepening, revisionist late phase of an oeuvre that began questioning its own myths with Unforgiven (1992). The film converges two charged geographies: the black volcanic sand of Iwo Jima, a speck of Japanese soil in the Pacific, and the half-remembered streets of an America where its general once dined among officers — homeland and enemy collapsing into a single psychological terrain of honor and dread. Its anchor is not a samurai but Saigo, a conscripted baker who carries the everyman's stubborn will to live where the warrior code demands death, a reluctant Sancho Panza who outlasts the knights around him. The Japanese sense of letters — 手紙, the intimate paper bridge between the dying and the living — frames a single lingering question: what survives of a man once his nation has decided he must not? Belonging to the rare humanist war film told entirely from the vanquished enemy's interior, shot almost wholly in Japanese, it pushes the combat genre past propaganda into something closer to requiem.

Sean S. Cunningham (b. 1941), a producer-turned-director who had cut his teeth assisting Wes Craven on the grimy provocation of The Last House on the Left (1972), arrived with a frankly commercial mission: to out-gross John Carpenter's Halloween (1978) on a shoestring. The result converges two American mythologies — the wholesome New England summer camp and the drowning-haunted lake — into a single space of arcadian dread, shot in the woods around Blairstown, New Jersey. Its protagonist, the watchful counselor Alice, descends from the Gothic 'final girl' lineage yet refuses the virginal saint, surviving less by purity than by exhausted, animal persistence. The title fixes a date of folk superstition — Friday the 13th — that promises misfortune without naming its agent, asking: is doom authored by a person, or simply by the calendar's arithmetic of inevitability? As the keystone of the post-Halloween slasher cycle, the film codified the body-count grammar, the killer's-eye camera, and the percussive sting that an entire 1980s subgenre would inherit. What does it mean that horror's most enduring engine was born not of metaphysics but of arithmetic and craft, and still terrifies?

Jean-Luc Godard (b. 1930), the most theoretically restless of the French New Wave's Cahiers du cinéma critics-turned-directors, made his feature debut here as a self-conscious vandal of classical grammar, and nothing in cinema's first sixty years quite prepared audiences for it. The film converges two symbolic geographies — the sun-bleached road from Marseille and the cafés, kiosks, and cramped hotel rooms of 1960 Paris — into a single drifting psychogeography where flight and stillness blur. Its protagonist, the petty thief Michel Poiccard, wears the trench coat and lip-rub of a Humphrey Bogart noir hero, yet he is an anti-Bogart who quotes the gangster mythos even as he empties it of gravity. The original title, À bout de souffle — literally "at the end of breath," out of wind, gasping — names not merely a man running from the law but a whole cinematic language exhaling its last: what does it mean to live, and to film, as if the next cut might erase you? Shot handheld by Raoul Coutard with a documentary looseness and edited into its notorious jump cuts, Breathless did not merely join the Nouvelle Vague — it became the movement's manifesto, detonating continuity itself and rewriting what a film could be.

Richard Linklater (b. 1960), the Austin-based laureate of American hangout cinema whose Dazed and Confused (1993) and Boyhood (2014) made the passage of time itself his subject, here returns to the mode he invented: plotless duration as profound form. The action unfolds across two ramshackle off-campus houses on the fringe of a 1980 Texas college town, where porch and dancefloor converge into a liminal threshold-space between adolescence and the institutions waiting beyond. At its center is Jake, an incoming freshman pitcher who recalls the wide-eyed wanderer-initiate of the bildungsroman — yet Linklater empties that arc of its crises, letting the boy simply drift and absorb rather than be tested. The title, lifted from Van Halen, insists everybody wants 'some' — but some of WHAT, in a weekend deliberately stripped of stakes, of girls, glory, transcendence, or merely the next moment before it vanishes? This is the apex of the so-called 'hangout film,' a subgenre Linklater all but authored, advancing it past nostalgia into a rigorous philosophy of presentness — a cinema that dares to find the meaning of a life in the time between the things that supposedly matter.

Sanjay Leela Bhansali (b. 1963), the most operatic stylist of contemporary Hindi cinema and heir to the maximalist melodrama of Mehboob Khan and Guru Dutt, mounted this third screen adaptation of Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay's 1917 novella as the most expensive Indian film of its time, a deliberate gesture toward total cinema where every frame strains under the weight of music, colour, and grief. Its world drifts between a fantasized turn-of-the-century Calcutta of zamindar mansions and the lamplit kotha of the courtesan, two spaces that converge into a single psychic architecture of longing held forever at a distance. At its centre is Devdas Mukherjee, an aristocratic prodigal who arrives wearing the mask of the returning hero and the doomed romantic lover, only to hollow out that archetype into something closer to a man in love with his own ruin. The title names not a story but a person dissolving into a verdict — what does it mean when a name becomes a synonym for self-destruction? As a culmination of the Bollywood musical melodrama, Devdas pushes the song-sequence and the saturated mise-en-scène past narrative into pure affect, and demands to be seen on the largest screen one can find.

Andy Muschietti (b. 1973), the Argentine horror stylist who broke out with Mamá (2013) and reframed Stephen King's 1986 doorstop into a two-part blockbuster, returns here to complete a project that sits at the crossroads of the modern Hollywood horror revival and the prestige-King adaptation lineage stretching back to Brian De Palma's Carrie (1976). The action unfolds between the fictional Maine hamlet of Derry and its mythic underbelly of sewers, drains, and the kissing bridge—an above-ground civility and a subterranean rot converging into a single psychological cartography of communal denial. At its center stands the grown Losers' Club, and especially the comedian Richie Tozier, a figure built on the archetype of the wisecracking jester whose jokes are armor, yet who quietly transcends it into something closer to an elegist. The very title, It Chapter Two, withholds a name, insisting the horror remain a pronoun, an it that refuses the dignity of naming—prompting the lingering question: what is the thing we cannot name because naming it would mean facing it? For admirers of post-2010 elevated and franchise horror alike, the film extends the coming-of-age-meets-cosmic-dread tradition into the terrain of adult memory and belated reckoning.

Billy Wilder (1906–2002), the Austrian-American émigré who fled Berlin's UFA studios for Hollywood and would master the corrosive comedy and the corrosive crime film with equal venom, made Double Indemnity at the moment his sardonic Mitteleuropa cynicism collided with American genre—a film often credited, alongside its co-writer Raymond Chandler's hardboiled prose, with codifying film noir itself. Its symbolic landscape is sun-bleached Los Angeles—the stucco Spanish-style Dietrichson house in Los Feliz and the fluorescent aisles of a Jerry's Market—where Mediterranean light becomes a cage of shadow, and the city of dreams curdles into a ledger of liabilities. Its protagonist, insurance salesman Walter Neff, arrives as the smooth American operator, a Faustian everyman who believes he can beat the system from the inside, only to discover he has been the mark all along. The title's phrase—an actuarial clause that pays twice for an unlikely death—turns the cold language of probability into the grammar of desire: what does it mean when love and murder are priced like a policy? Advancing the nascent noir cycle from atmosphere into architecture, this is the film that taught the genre how to confess.

Robert Bresson (b. 1901–d. 1999), the austere French master of what he termed cinématographie — the rigorous purgation of theatrical acting in favor of the 'model,' the flat affect, the fragmented gesture — closes his career with this 1983 adaptation of Tolstoy's novella 'The Forged Coupon,' his final and most pitiless film. Its world is a Parisian circuit of bourgeois photo-shops and provincial farmhouses, spaces that converge into a single moral economy where commerce and condemnation are the same transaction. At its center moves Yvon, a fuel-oil deliveryman who recalls the wronged everyman of naturalist tragedy — a Job stripped of any answering voice — yet who curdles into something the archetype refuses to be. The title L'Argent ('Money') names not a possession but a circulating agent, a force that passes through hands and erases the faces above them: what becomes of guilt when its medium is anonymous and infinitely transferable? Heir to Bresson's own Pickpocket (1959) and Au hasard Balthazar (1966), L'Argent stands as the severe terminus of his spiritual minimalism, advancing the cinema of transcendental style toward its coldest, most materialist limit — a film that watches grace withdraw and never returns.

Alain Resnais (1922–2014), the French essayist-filmmaker who emerged from the documentary tradition (Night and Fog, 1956) before becoming the Left Bank conscience of the Nouvelle Vague, here makes his first feature an act of formal heresy: cinema as the architecture of memory. The film binds two impossible places—the rebuilt, neon-rinsed Hiroshima walked until dawn and the medieval French town of Nevers glimpsed only in a cellar's damp and a river's drift—until geography dissolves into a single psychic terrain where catastrophe and intimacy share one skin. Its protagonist, a French actress (Emmanuelle Riva) come to play a part in a peace film, recalls the confessional wanderer of melodrama only to shatter that mold, becoming instead an unreliable archive of her own grief. The very title, Hiroshima mon amour, fuses an annihilated city to a lover's endearment, an obscene tenderness that opens onto its great Hwadu: can one remember another's suffering, or only one's own, and is forgetting a betrayal or a mercy? Written by novelist Marguerite Duras and cut with the radical splices that would define the modernist memory-film, it remains the foundational text of cinema's break with linear time.

Robert Hamer (b. 1911), the most literate and saturnine of the Ealing Studios directors, brought to comedy a moral coldness closer to Stendhal than to slapstick, and Kind Hearts and Coronets stands as the apex of that brief, doomed brilliance before drink and disrepute ended him. Its England is mapped between two converging poles — the inviolable family mausoleum that bars a mother's body, and the gentlemanly prison cell where a condemned man writes — fusing into a single space where class and death keep the same ledger. Its protagonist, Louis Mazzini, is a Raskolnikov in spats: the wronged outsider who reasons his way to murder, yet who replaces the Russian's fevered guilt with a perfect, amused serenity. The very title, lifted from Tennyson — that 'Kind hearts are more than coronets, / And simple faith than Norman blood' — is wielded as exquisite irony, asking whether anything beneath the manners is true at all: is breeding virtue, or merely the costume murder wears? As the supreme achievement of the Ealing comedy, it advances the form by turning English understatement itself into the instrument of homicide, proving that the most lethal weapon in the realm is good manners.

Debra Granik (b. 1963), the American director whose Winter's Bone (2010) made the rural margins of the United States into a register of poetic, anthropological precision, returns here in a vein that extends the regional realism of Kelly Reichardt and the Dardenne brothers while softening their fatalism into something close to grace. Her landscape is Forest Park near Portland, Oregon — a wilderness improbably folded inside a city's limits — set against the monitored housing, screens, and intake offices of the welfare state, so that 'inside' and 'outside' become a single contested psychic terrain. At the center is Will, a war veteran and survivalist father raising his daughter Tom off the grid, a figure who recalls the wandering hermit-patriarch of American myth yet quietly refuses that lineage's heroism. The title's deceptively practical phrase — the camper's creed to 'leave no trace' — slowly turns inward: what does it cost a person to pass through the world leaving no mark, and can love survive invisibility? Filmed in the slow-cinema, post-mumblecore key of contemporary American social realism, the film advances that tradition by treating tenderness, not trauma, as its true subject — a study of attachment, dignity, and the unbearable arithmetic of letting go.

Denis Villeneuve (b. 1967), the French-Canadian architect of cerebral spectacle whose Sicario and Arrival fused art-house patience with blockbuster scale, here inherits the most intimidating legacy in science fiction, accepting a torch lit by Ridley Scott in 1982. The film unfolds across two converging zones: a perpetually raining Los Angeles drowned in towering holographic advertising, and an irradiated, ochre-dead San Diego wasteland and a Las Vegas embalmed in orange dust—exterior ruin standing in for interior emptiness. Its protagonist, the LAPD blade runner known only as Officer K (Ryan Gosling), arrives as the classic noir detective hunting a buried truth, yet quietly subverts the archetype: the hunter who may be the very thing he hunts, the orphan questing for an origin that may not be his. The numerical title 2049 names not a year but a deadline, a countdown stamped on a manufactured life, posing its Hwadu: can a being engineered to serve choose meaning the world refuses to grant it? Advancing the neo-noir and cyberpunk tradition while deepening it into a meditation on memory, labor, and personhood, this is tech-noir as philosophy, and it demands the full attention it so generously rewards.

Stanley Kubrick (b. 1928) — the Bronx-born perfectionist whose films from Paths of Glory (1957) to Barry Lyndon (1975) treat war and institutions as immaculate machines grinding human beings into geometry — here delivers his penultimate work, the coldest and most clinical of his late period. The fiction unfolds across Parris Island and the rubble of Hue, yet both converge into a single symbolic geography: the parade ground and the burning city become one continuous corridor through which men are processed, named, and discharged. At its center stands Private Joker, a combat correspondent in the mold of the wisecracking everyman-survivor, an archetype he steadily hollows out until observation itself becomes complicity. The English title 'Full Metal Jacket' names the bullet's copper sheath — the casing that keeps soft lead from deforming on impact, the better to pierce a body cleanly — and so poses its Hwadu: what does it cost a man to be encased, made hard enough to kill without splintering? Advancing the Vietnam war film beyond the operatic delirium of Apocalypse Now toward something nearer to procedural anatomy, Kubrick refuses catharsis and dares the genre to admit it was always about the manufacture of killers.

Abbas Kiarostami (b. 1940), the Iranian master whose Koker trilogy and Palme d'Or-winning Taste of Cherry redefined cinema's relationship to the long take, the windshield, and the porous border between fiction and life, here makes his final feature far from home — his first shot entirely in Japan, after Certified Copy's Tuscan experiment in role-play. Tokyo's anonymous neon corridors and the hushed interior of a book-lined apartment converge into a single membrane of looking, a city that surrounds without admitting. At its center is Akiko, a student-escort who recalls the literary type of the woman mistaken for someone else — the Galatea, the projection screen — only to dissolve that archetype as no one's reading of her quite holds. The title Like Someone in Love hinges on that fragile 'like': not love but its resemblance, performance shading into feeling. Who is actually loved when everyone loves a likeness? Extending the Iranian New Wave's meta-fictional inquiry onto foreign soil, this is a quietly radical advance in the cinema of the unreliable surface — proof that Kiarostami's interrogation of image and identity needed no native tongue.

Greta Gerwig (b. 1983), the mumblecore-bred actor turned auteur whose Lady Bird announced a poet of overlapping voices and unsentimental tenderness, returns with her most formally audacious feature, transmuting Louisa May Alcott's 1868–69 perennial into a recursive object of cinematic time. The film converges two symbolic landscapes: Concord, Massachusetts, the Transcendentalist heartland of Emerson and Thoreau where domestic warmth glows golden, and a colder, bluer Paris and New York where ambition is priced and weighed. Its protagonist, the writer Jo March, arrives in the lineage of the Künstlerroman heroine — a Brontë-esque rebel — but transcends the type by refusing to let her story be the property of anyone but herself. The title Little Women carries its old condescension like a blade turned outward: who decides what is little, and what is the market price of a woman's life? Gerwig advances the literary-adaptation tradition and the contemporary feminist costume drama by fusing them with achronological, memory-structured montage, making the heritage film argue with its own nostalgia. To watch it is to feel period cinema think.

George Miller (b. 1945), the Australian former physician who launched Ozploitation's most enduring myth with 1979's Mad Max, returns after thirty years not as a nostalgist but as an avant-garde action choreographer, his style now a percussive symphony of centered framing, undercranked motion, and practical pyrotechnics that rebukes the digital incoherence of contemporary blockbusters. Across the irradiated wasteland between the Citadel's aquifer cliffs and the receding mirage of the 'Green Place,' a real Namibian desert becomes a psychological theater of scarcity, fertility, and ecological grief. Into this barrels Imperator Furiosa, a one-armed war captain who arrives dressed as the lone gunslinger of frontier legend only to dismantle that archetype from within, ceding nothing of her interiority to the muzzled wanderer beside her. The title invokes 'fury' as both rage and momentum—but whose road is it, and toward what redemption does a road that only doubles back lead? As a landmark of the post-apocalyptic chase film and feminist genre revisionism, Fury Road proves that spectacle, stripped to its mythic bone and shot in-camera, can still carry the full weight of allegory.

Joseph L. Mankiewicz (b. 1909), the rare double Academy Award winner for writing and directing who prized dialogue as a weapon and conversation as combat, made All About Eve at the apex of a screenwriter's cinema, a literate counter-tradition to spectacle that runs back through Lubitsch's verbal wit. Its world spans the gilded banquet of the Sarah Siddons Society and the cramped backstage dressing room of a Broadway theater—public altar and private confessional fused into a single anatomy of ambition. At its center is Eve Harrington, the worshipful fan recast as understudy, a figure who wears the mask of the grateful Cinderella only to invert it into something colder and more Machiavellian. The title promises total disclosure—everything about Eve—yet the more the film reveals, the more it asks: can a self assembled entirely from performance ever be known, or is there only the next role beneath the last? Arriving in 1950 as Hollywood eyed television with dread and as the studio system began to crack, this remains the supreme example of the backstage chamber drama, advancing the all-talking, all-cutting comedy of manners into a tragedy about the theater devouring its young.

Charlie Kaufman (b. 1958), the screenwriter-turned-director whose Being John Malkovich, Adaptation and Synecdoche, New York made cerebral self-erasure his signature, here adapts Iain Reid's 2016 novel into perhaps the most ruthlessly interiorized work of his career, the apotheosis of his lifelong project to film consciousness from the inside out. Two spaces converge into one psychological membrane: the snow-blind interstate of rural Oklahoma and an isolated family farmhouse whose basement stays locked, until landscape and architecture dissolve into a single weather-system of mind. At its center moves Jessie Buckley's nameless woman — ostensibly the dutiful girlfriend meeting the parents, a road-trip companion in the lineage of the patient muse, yet she curdles that archetype into something far stranger and more sovereign. The title's gerund, 'I'm Thinking of Ending Things,' hovers between a wish to leave a relationship and something vaster and final — and asks: whose thought are we inside, and what exactly does that voice wish to end? For admirers of the metaphysical art film and the surrealist memory-cinema of Resnais and Lynch, this is the form pushed to its solipsistic extremity — a chamber piece where the chamber is a skull, and every room another decade.

Alex van Warmerdam (b. 1952), the Dutch painter-turned-auteur whose deadpan absurdist tableaux (Abel, The Northerners, The Last Days of Emma Blank) extend a Lowlands tradition of mordant unease stretching back to Bosch and Bruegel, here crafts his most internationally celebrated provocation — the first Dutch film in Cannes' main competition in nearly four decades. Its symbolic landscape converges a pristine modernist glass house on a manicured suburban lawn with the damp, root-tangled forest floor from which an underground hideout emerges, a Vermeer-clean interior haunted by the soil beneath it. At its center stands Camiel Borgman, a courteous bearded vagrant who recalls the archetype of the diabolical guest — Pasolini's Visitor in Teorema, the trickster who unhouses the bourgeoisie — yet who refuses every theological or psychological key offered him. The very title, a surname that names nothing, withholds: who, or what, is Borgman, and why does a family's politeness become the instrument of its undoing? For admirers of the European art-horror and bourgeois-nightmare tradition — Haneke's Funny Games, Buñuel's class fables — this is a vital, glacial advance: horror without a single shock cue, terror dispensed with a smile.

Roland Emmerich (b. 1955), the German-born showman of spectacle-disaster who turned the destruction of monuments into a Hollywood signature with Independence Day (1996), The Day After Tomorrow (2004) and 2012 (2009), returns here to the genre he helped codify, twenty years on. The terrain spans a moon converted into a forward military bastion and the Atlantic seaboard swallowed by a continent-sized shadow — two zones converging into a single symbolic space where humanity is at once colonizer and colonized. At its center stands Patricia Whitmore, presidential aide and pilot, a Telemachus-figure inheriting a father's war who refuses to remain merely the legatee. The title — Resurgence — names not just an alien return but the compulsion of a culture to relive its own triumph; what does it mean for a generation to be raised inside the memory of a victory it never won? As a late entry in the post-9/11 globalized blockbuster and the cycle of legacy-sequels, this film advances the disaster spectacle into the era of franchise inheritance, where the apocalypse itself has become heritage.

Noah Baumbach (b. 1969), the New York miniaturist of articulate familial wounds whose career arcs from the verbal warfare of The Squid and the Whale (2005) through Frances Ha (2012) and Marriage Story (2019), here trades Manhattan brownstones for the rolling anonymity of a continent, his most expansive and most elegiac film to date. Its symbolic landscape converges the European sleeper train and the gilded awards podium into a single corridor of motion that never arrives — a moving room between a life lived and a life applauded. At its center is Jay Kelly, an aging movie star played by George Clooney, who begins as the familiar archetype of the celebrity in midlife crisis only to dissolve that figure into something stranger: a man who can no longer locate the seam between his performances and his soul. The very ordinariness of the title 'Jay Kelly' — a name as blank and ownable as a marquee — poses its lingering Hwadu: when a face has belonged to everyone, who is left to wear it home? Advancing the late-career star-as-subject elegy that runs from Wild Strawberries to Birdman, Baumbach makes the road movie a vehicle for reckoning with the self as its own back catalogue.

Martin Scorsese (b. 1942), the Italian-American chronicler of male violence and Catholic guilt who had just announced himself with Mean Streets (1973), here makes his most improbable and underrated work — a studio-assigned, Ellen Burstyn-driven women's picture that he turned into a sly, restless deconstruction of the form. Its symbolic geography runs from the candy-colored soundstage of a vanished California to the dust and chrome of Tucson, Arizona, two Americas — the mythic and the actual — pressing against each other on the same road. At its center is Alice Hyatt, a widowed mother and would-be singer who arrives looking like the road-movie dreamer or the resilient Hollywood heroine, only to keep colliding with a reality those archetypes were built to erase. The title, deceptively casual, asks who exactly the Alice of the past tense was, and whether she ever lived 'here' at all: where does a woman go when the self she was promised never arrives? Emerging in the shadow of second-wave feminism and the New Hollywood, the film stands as a foundational entry in the 1970s feminist road movie, redirecting Scorsese's signature kinetic energy toward a question the macho cinema of the decade rarely dared to pose.

Rob Reiner (b. 1947), the genially versatile American director who moved from the affectionate pastiche of This Is Spinal Tap and the coming-of-age tenderness of Stand By Me to the swooning romanticism of When Harry Met Sally, here pivots into pure dread, marshalling his unfashionable classicism in service of Stephen King's tightest premise. The action contracts from a snowbound stretch of the Colorado Rockies into the suffocating farmhouse interior of Annie Wilkes, until landscape and psyche fuse into a single white prison where escape and burial look identical. At its centre lies Paul Sheldon, a bestselling novelist (embodied by James Caan) who enters as the rescued invalid of melodrama only to invert that archetype, becoming a Scheherazade in reverse — a storyteller who must keep writing not to delay another's death but his own. The title's single word, 'Misery,' names at once the doomed heroine of his potboilers, the condition of his captivity, and the wound at the root of all narrative: must the artist suffer, and serve, to create? William Goldman's screenplay sharpens King's confessional allegory into a chamber thriller that advances the psychological-horror tradition by locating terror not in the monstrous but in the adoring — the most domestic, most devoted face imaginable.

John Francis Daley (b. 1985)—the former child actor of NBC's Freaks and Geeks turned screenwriter of Horrible Bosses, here co-directing with Jonathan Goldstein his first studio feature—brings an unexpected formal rigor to the American studio comedy, importing the kinetic camera grammar of the modern action thriller into the suburban living room. The film unfolds across two converging worlds: the cul-de-sac, that quintessential American emblem of contained middle-class aspiration, and a glass-walled modernist mansion of underworld luxury, the two folding into a single board-game diorama rendered in shrinking tilt-shift focus. At its center is Max, a competitive everyman husband in the Cary Grant 'wrong man' tradition—the ordinary fellow plunged into intrigue he cannot decode—except here the intrigue may be a fiction he is too eager to play. The title Game Night names not an event but an ontology: when does play stop being play, and who decides? If the rules are invisible, how do you know you are still inside the game? As a contribution to the post-Apatow comedy and the revival of the screwball thriller hybrid, the film advances its genre by treating slapstick with the visual seriousness of Fincher, proving the studio comedy can still be directed rather than merely shot.

John Hughes (b. 1950), the Michigan-bred chronicler of suburban adolescence whose run from Sixteen Candles (1984) through The Breakfast Club (1985) made him the laureate of Reagan-era teendom, here loosens his confessional realism into something closer to fable and direct address. The film converges two registers of Chicago into one psychic geography: the institutional cage of a North Shore high school and the gleaming downtown of the Art Institute, the Sears Tower, and Wrigley Field, where civic spectacle becomes a stage for desire. Its protagonist, the senior Ferris Bueller, arrives looking like the trickster of folklore—the Lord of Misrule, the holiday-king who suspends the ordinary order—yet he subverts that archetype by demanding the audience join his game. The title's lazy promise of a 'Day Off' conceals a sharper idea: a day not merely free of labor but stolen from time itself. What is a single day worth against the dread of the future closing in? Standing within the teen comedy as Hughes virtually invented it, this 1986 work pushes the genre toward metacinema and philosophical comedy, smuggling Epicurean and existential anxieties inside a Paramount summer hit aimed squarely at the multiplex.

Joe Russo (b. 1971), who with his brother Anthony migrated from the comic sitcom rhythms of Arrested Development and Community into the engine room of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, here makes the franchise's most paranoid and politically literate entry, a deliberate homage to the conspiracy cinema of Alan J. Pakula and Sydney Pollack. Its Washington, D.C.—the Smithsonian's marble galleries colliding with the Potomac's looming Triskelion headquarters—becomes less a capital than a panopticon, a psychic terrain where memory and surveillance contest the same ground. At its center stands Steve Rogers, the super-soldier out of time, drawn as the incorruptible Boy Scout knight only to have that very purity weaponized against the institution he serves, an Arthurian loyalist forced to betray Camelot to save it. The title's 'Winter Soldier' carries Thomas Paine's bitter 1776 phrase about the man who shrinks in crisis, inverted into a frozen instrument of a state that fears its own future: what does freedom mean when security demands the murder of who you might become? As a superhero film it advances the political-thriller hybrid, proving the blockbuster could metabolize Snowden-era anxieties without surrendering its kinetic, practical-stunt spectacle.

Savanah Leaf (b. 1993), a British-American filmmaker and former Olympic volleyball player whose video work with Gary Clark Jr. and her own short Earth Mama (2020) signaled a documentarian's eye for the unscripted face, makes her narrative feature debut in a register closer to the neorealist hush of the Dardenne brothers than to American social-issue drama. Here Oakland's freeway underpasses and the soft eucalyptus dusk of the East Bay converge into a single symbolic terrain where institutional surveillance and the indifferent beauty of California light occupy the same frame. Her protagonist, Gia — a pregnant single mother photographing other families' happiness in a mall studio — recalls the archetype of the sacrificial maternal figure, yet refuses the genre's appetite for either martyrdom or redemption arc. The title Earth Mama gathers the ancient iconography of the fertile, all-giving mother and sets it against a present in which the state weighs that very fertility as risk: who decides which mothers are permitted to mother? Advancing the contemporary current of poetic American realism — the lineage of Barry Jenkins and Andrew Dosunmu, on whose work Leaf's cinematographer trained — this is a film that listens where others would explain.

Im Kwon-taek (b. 1936), the indefatigable patriarch of Korean cinema whose hundred-plus films span the painterly mysticism of Mandala (1981) and the agonized artistry of Chihwaseon (2002), here turns his late-career mastery toward the nation's deepest folk inheritance. The riverside Gwanghallu pavilion of Namwon and the cloistered torture-yard of a provincial governor's compound converge into a single charged space where Confucian propriety and forbidden desire share one wall. At its center stands Chunhyang, the courtesan's daughter who reads like a Korean Penelope—steadfast, besieged, fending off a suitor's coercion—yet who refuses to be merely the patient wife awaiting her lord. The title bears her name alone, neither lover nor master attached: what does it mean to make an entire epic the property of a low-born woman's name? Crucially, Im frames the whole tale through pansori—the centuries-old solo sung narrative recognized by UNESCO—so that the film is at once a costume drama and a recording of a live performance. As both heritage-cinema and a radical experiment in turning folk-opera into screen grammar, Chunhyang advances Im's lifelong project of forging a distinctly Korean film language from indigenous art forms.

Jim Jarmusch (b. 1953), the patron saint of American independent cinema whose deadpan minimalism — from Stranger Than Paradise (1984) to Dead Man (1995) — turned languor into a moral stance, here grafts his downtown New York cool onto a meditation on duty and obsolescence. The film's unnamed city, all cracked rooftops and vacant lots, fuses the post-industrial decay of the American Rust Belt with the spectral codes of feudal Edo Japan, so that a pigeon coop becomes a watchtower and a curbside ice-cream truck a roadside teahouse. Its protagonist, a hulking Black assassin called Ghost Dog, plays as a rōnin in the lineage of Kurosawa's masterless swordsmen and Alain Delon's glacial killer in Le Samouraï — yet he subverts the archetype by serving a master who has forgotten he exists. The title's invocation of 'the Way of the Samurai' (drawn from the eighteenth-century Hagakure) frames a haunting Hwadu: can a code give meaning to a life the world no longer has any use for? Welding the Jim Jarmusch art film to the gangster picture and the chambara samurai genre, scored by RZA in his cinematic debut, the film stands as a landmark of hip-hop-era genre hybridity.

Alfonso Cuarón (b. 1961), the Mexican auteur whose long-take metaphysics in Y tu mamá también (2001) and later Gravity (2013) made the unbroken shot a moral instrument rather than mere bravura, here delivers the keystone of his early-twenty-first-century work alongside cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki. The film converges a bombed, cage-strewn London with the fenced seaside detention zone of Bexhill, fusing the imperial metropole and the refugee camp into a single psychic terrain where civilization's end is administrative rather than apocalyptic. Its protagonist, Theo Faron, a burnt-out former activist turned bureaucratic drone, begins as the disenchanted Everyman of dystopian fiction—heir to Winston Smith—only to transcend the type by rediscovering custodianship without ideology. The very title, drawn from Psalm 90's lament that God turns men to destruction saying 'Return, ye children of men,' poses its Hwadu: if no future arrives, what remains worth carrying through the ruins? Arriving amid the post-9/11 surveillance state and Europe's hardening borders, Children of Men advances the dystopian-realist subgenre by stripping science fiction of spectacle, shooting catastrophe in documentary grey, and proving that the genre's deepest terror is not the future's strangeness but its banal familiarity.

Todd Phillips (b. 1970), the American filmmaker who pivoted from the gross-out anarchy of The Hangover to the Scorsese-haunted character study of Joker (2019), returns to the comic-book idiom only to detonate it from within, crafting an anti-sequel that refuses the franchise machine it belongs to. The fluorescent corridors of Arkham State Hospital and the camera-thronged spectacle of a Gotham courtroom converge into a single carceral theatre where the line between cell and stage dissolves. At its center is Arthur Fleck (Joaquin Phoenix), a janitor-turned-icon who recalls the doomed showman of Pagliacci yet inverts that archetype, performing not to mask his pain but to learn whether he ever wanted the mask at all. The subtitle's clinical French — folie à deux, the shared delusion of two — frames a romance with fellow patient Lee Quinzel as a contagion of belief, and leaves a question hanging like a held note: when the world has fallen in love with a legend, is the man beneath it permitted to exist? Drawing on the classical Hollywood musical, the courtroom drama, and the psychological prison film, the picture advances the deconstructive comic-book cinema that Joker pioneered, weaponizing genre to interrogate its own fandom.

Haruo Sotozaki (b. 1978), the Ufotable director whose digitally-painted compositing fused 2D character animation with volumetric CGI environments across the Demon Slayer franchise, here arrives at the climactic theatrical chapter of an oeuvre built on making hand-drawn swordsmanship breathe inside computer-rendered space. The film's symbolic landscape draws on two converging vectors: the floating, gravity-defying architecture of the Infinity Castle, descended from Edo-era ukiyo-e interiors, and the wisteria flower (fuji), Japan's ancient emblem of both poison and remembrance. At its center stands Tanjiro Kamado, voiced by Natsuki Hanae—a hero cast in the lineage of the compassionate bodhisattva, yet who subverts the shōnen warrior by refusing to hate even what he must destroy. The very title, Infinity Castle (Mugen-jō), names a place without exit, a labyrinth of endless rooms—but is a prison built of infinity still a prison, or has the boundary between hunter and hunted dissolved into something stranger? For devotees of the post-Akira anime renaissance and the contemporary kaiju-scaled action film, this entry pushes the limit-experiment of digital traditional animation toward operatic tragedy, proving the medium can hold both spectacle and elegy in a single frame.

Deniz Gamze Ergüven (b. 1978), a Turkish-French filmmaker trained at France's prestigious La Fémis, made her feature debut with a work that fuses the lyrical naturalism of the Yeşilçam-descended Turkish art cinema with the sun-bleached female-collective poetics of Sofia Coppola's The Virgin Suicides; co-written with Alice Winocour, it earned a 2016 Academy Award nomination for Best Foreign Language Film. Its world stretches between a remote village on Turkey's Black Sea coast near Inebolu and the shimmering rumor of Istanbul, two poles that harden into a single psychic geography of confinement and the open road. At its center stands Lale, the youngest of five orphaned sisters, who begins as a wide-eyed innocent in the mold of the captive fairy-tale daughter and quietly mutates into something fiercer — a strategist of escape. The title, Mustang, names no horse onscreen; it imports a foreign word for an untamed creature, and asks: can wildness be inherited, contained, or only outrun? Arriving amid a global resurgence of feminist auteur cinema and the post-Arab-Spring reckoning with patriarchal authority, the film advances the coming-of-age genre into something closer to insurrection.

Kelly Reichardt (b. 1964), the Miami-born high priestess of American slow cinema and a defining voice in the Pacific Northwest's regional realism, returns with a film that distills her gentle, durational minimalism—honed across Old Joy and Meek's Cutoff—into its purest form. Here the dripping Oregon forest and the muddy banks of the Columbia River converge into a symbolic borderland where wilderness and nascent commerce press against one another, a frontier not of glory but of mud and milk. At its center stands Cookie Figowitz, a soft-handed cook who at first recalls the lonely Western drifter of John Ford and Anthony Mann, only to quietly invert that archetype: he is a maker, a gatherer, a nurturer in a genre built on guns. The title's deceptive plainness—First Cow—announces an origin myth, the very first of something in a virgin territory, and lingers on a question: what exactly is born when the first capital arrives in Eden? Reichardt advances the revisionist Western and the burgeoning idiom of anti-capitalist American art cinema, proving that tenderness, friendship, and a fried cake can carry the full weight of a nation's founding sin.

Chris Columbus (b. 1958), the populist craftsman of Home Alone and later the Harry Potter franchise, refines here his signature mode — the wounded family melodrama smuggled inside broad commercial comedy — into its most emotionally engineered form. Set against a San Francisco of Victorian row houses and family courthouses, the city's bohemian openness collides with the cold architecture of custody law, fashioning a psychological space where domestic warmth and bureaucratic exile share a single address. At its center is Daniel Hillard, an unemployed voice actor (Robin Williams), who begins as the eternal Trickster-clown only to mutate into something stranger: a father who must become a fiction to be allowed near his own children. The title's borrowed dignity — 'Doubtfire,' a name plucked from a newspaper headline — masks a question that lingers long after the laughter: must a man disguise his love to be permitted to give it? Arriving at the high-water mark of the early-1990s Hollywood family comedy, the film advances the cross-dressing farce tradition of Some Like It Hot and Tootsie toward a melancholy register few of its imitators reached, weaponizing slapstick in service of the era's quiet anxiety about the broken American household.

Chris Columbus (b. 1958), the John Hughes protégé who graduated from screenwriting Gremlins to defining the family blockbuster, here works at the seam between the Spielbergian suburban fable and the broad slapstick of silent comedy, crafting what would become the highest-grossing live-action comedy of its era. Its world condenses around two converging poles: an affluent red-brick house in Winnetka on Chicago's North Shore and the snow-laced, departure-board chaos of O'Hare and Paris, so that home and exile press against one another within a single Christmas. At its center is Kevin McCallister, an eight-year-old who begins as the overlooked youngest child of fairy-tale neglect and becomes a pint-sized Odysseus defending his own Ithaca, a child Crusoe improvising civilization from a deserted domestic island. The very title, Home Alone, holds its paradox taut — is the home a sanctuary or a trap, and is solitude a punishment or the first taste of selfhood? Standing at the crossroads of the holiday film and the home-invasion thriller, it advances the family comedy by smuggling Grand Guignol and existential abandonment beneath its tinsel, asking what a house is when emptied of everyone who made it home.

Majid Majidi (b. 1959), the Iranian director who emerged from the post-revolutionary New Wave alongside Abbas Kiarostami and Jafar Panahi, here refines a humanist neorealism into something nearly devotional, his camera kneeling at child-height to find the sacred in the threadbare. Between the cramped walled lanes of poor south Tehran and the gleaming hilltop villas of the wealthy north, the film constructs a vertical moral geography — a single bus ride that doubles as a chasm. Its protagonist, nine-year-old Ali, is cast in the mould of the wandering child-witness of De Sica's neorealism, the boy who shoulders an adult's burden, yet he transcends the type: he is less victim than secret penitent, racing not from poverty but toward redemption. The Persian title, Bacheha-ye Aseman — 'children of heaven' — gathers the dust of the alley and the light of the sky into one phrase, asking whether innocence is a possession the poor are permitted to keep, or the only wealth they truly own. For anyone tracing the lineage of Iranian cinema after the 1979 revolution, when censorship pushed filmmakers toward children's stories and ethical parable, this is the movement at its most luminous and morally exacting.

Andrew Adamson (b. 1966), the New Zealand visual-effects supervisor turned director who cut his teeth on The Mask before co-helming this DreamWorks landmark, arrived at feature filmmaking as a technician-iconoclast positioned squarely against the Disney hegemony Jeffrey Katzenberg had abandoned. The film's geography splits between two converging fictions: the pristine, walled town of Duloc, a topiary-perfect theme park of order, and the fetid swamp on its margins, a psychological lowland of repressed appetite and exile. At its center stands Shrek, an ogre cast in the mold of the fairy-tale monster who guards the tower—yet he inverts the archetype, becoming the rescuer, the lover, the wounded hermit whose gruffness shields tenderness. The title is a single barked syllable, derived from the Yiddish 'shrek' meaning terror or fright, an onomatopoeia of revulsion: what does it mean when the thing that frightens turns out to be the thing most worthy of love? As a foundational text of the post-Disney CGI fairy-tale satire—the subgenre it practically invented—Shrek advanced computer animation into the realm of cultural critique, weaponizing the form against the very studio mythology that birthed it.

Bryan Singer (b. 1965), the American director who detonated his reputation with this sophomore feature before a fraught Hollywood career, here works in the cool, architectural neo-noir register that the early 1990s independent boom—Soderbergh, Tarantino, the Sundance-to-studio pipeline—had made commercially electric, fusing the labyrinthine plotting of classic studio noir with the verbal pyrotechnics of Christopher McQuarrie's screenplay. The film converges two charged American spaces: a fluorescent Los Angeles interrogation room and the burning maritime sprawl of San Pedro harbor, the one a chamber of confession, the other a pyre that consumes its own evidence. At its center sits Roger 'Verbal' Kint, a stammering crippled witness who recalls the noir patsy and the unreliable confessor of Wilkie Collins and Conrad, only to dismantle that archetype from within. The title's 'usual suspects'—Captain Renault's throwaway order in Casablanca—asks who is rounded up, who is overlooked, and what it costs to be underestimated: when a face is studied, is the man ever truly seen? For lovers of the puzzle-film and the unreliable-narrator thriller, this is the work that recalibrated the modern twist ending and taught a generation of cinema how a story can be a weapon.

Pete Docter (b. 1968), the Pixar animator-turned-director who would later co-author the studio's metaphysical maturity with Inside Out (2015) and Soul (2020), here makes his most disarmingly elegiac feature, a balloon-borne adventure that conceals a treatise on mourning beneath candy-bright surfaces. Its symbolic geography pivots between a clapboard American house dwarfed by encroaching skyscrapers and the towering tepuis of Venezuela's Canaima region—Mount Roraima reimagined as Paradise Falls—so that domestic stasis and untouched wilderness become two faces of a single grief. Its protagonist, the square-jawed widower Carl Fredricksen, arrives looking like the curmudgeon archetype of countless comedies, only to dismantle that cliché into something closer to a Tennysonian Ulysses too late for his own voyage. The single word of the title, Up, names not merely altitude but the impossible direction of all longing—the lift away from earth, age, and loss—and asks: can a life finally rise only once it agrees to let go of what anchors it? As a landmark of computer-animated family cinema, it advances the Pixar tradition of smuggling adult devastation into all-ages spectacle, proving the medium capable of genuine threnody.

Kim Ki-duk (b. 1960), the self-taught provocateur of South Korean cinema who emerged from the figurative-painting margins to become the country's most extreme moral fabulist — author of The Isle (2000), Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter… and Spring (2003) and 3-Iron (2004) — here delivers the film that won the 2012 Venice Golden Lion, a late-career pivot from monastic silence to the howl of capital. Its world is forged where Seoul's Cheonggyecheon stream, once buried under expressway concrete and then symbolically restored, gives way to the soot-black machine shops of small fabricators awaiting the wrecking ball — a topography where flowing water and grinding lathe become one psychic space. Its protagonist, the loan-shark enforcer Kang-do, arrives as a kind of demonic Raskolnikov, an instrument of debt who seems beyond redemption until something more ancient than guilt is loosed in him. The title invokes Michelangelo's Pietà, the Virgin cradling her dead son — yet who, here, cradles whom, and can a mother's body purchase back a soul priced in won? This is the apex of the Korean 'extreme' art-cinema lineage, fusing Christian iconography with the cruelty of the post-IMF debt economy into something unbearably tender and merciless at once.

Jon Watts (b. 1981), the indie noir stylist of Cop Car who was recruited into the Marvel Cinematic Universe to humanize its most overexposed property, here treats the comic-book blockbuster as a John Hughes coming-of-age comedy in disguise, threading Spielbergian suburban wonder through corporate spectacle. The film stages itself between two converging Americas: the gleaming Avengers Tower of Manhattan and the working-class stoops, fire escapes, and bodegas of Queens — wealth and labor pressed against the same skyline. Its protagonist, Peter Parker, is the eternal adolescent everyman, a Holden Caulfield with web-shooters, yet he subverts that archetype by being defined less by alienation than by an almost desperate eagerness to belong to institutions that may not deserve him. The very word 'Homecoming' carries a triple charge — a high-school dance, a franchise reclaiming a lost character, and a question about where a boy who lives between two worlds can ever truly arrive home; what, the film asks, does one owe the place and the people who made you? As the definitive teen-superhero hybrid, it advances the MCU's tonal experiment by proving the genre can shrink to the scale of a sophomore's longing without losing its weight.

Park Chan-wook (b. 1963), the South Korean stylist whose baroque compositions and moral vertigo would soon make Oldboy a Cannes sensation, here opens what becomes his Vengeance Trilogy with its coldest, most rigorously austere chapter — a film that strips revenge of the operatic catharsis his later work would supply. Its world unfolds between the anonymous concrete of a Seoul factory district and a deceptively serene green riverbank, two poles that converge into a single landscape where industrial cruelty and pastoral peace become indistinguishable. At its center stands Ryu, a deaf factory worker recalling the holy fool or righteous avenger of classical tragedy, yet who subverts that archetype: he is neither hero nor villain but a node in a circuit of grief that has no moral exit. The original Korean title, Boksuneun naui geot — 'Vengeance is Mine' — quotes scripture's claim that retribution belongs to God alone, then hands it to men who can only botch it. Who, then, is the 'Mr.' the title pities, when everyone is both perpetrator and mourner? A landmark of the Korean New Wave's turn toward the morally pitiless thriller, the film advances revenge cinema by refusing it the consolation of justice.

Felipe Gálvez Haberle (b. 1983), a Chilean filmmaker steeped in the political austerity of the New Chilean Cinema that followed Pablo Larraín and Sebastián Lelio, makes his feature debut with the formal severity of a history painting and the patience of Carlos Reygadas. His canvas is Tierra del Fuego and the broader sweep of Patagonia, where the endless windswept grasslands of the Selk'nam homelands collide with the surveyed perimeters of José Menéndez's pastoral empire, fusing geography and ledger into a single psychic terrain of conquest. Across it rides Segundo, a mestizo marksman hired for his rifle — at first glance the laconic gunman of the classic Western, yet a figure who quietly inverts that archetype, the dispossessed forced to aim at his own reflection. The title — Los colonos, 'The Settlers,' those who claim land by settling it — turns a neutral noun into an indictment, posing its lingering Hwadu: when atrocity is rewritten as nation-building, who is permitted to remember, and in whose language? Reviving and dismantling the revisionist Western through a Latin American anticolonial lens, the film advances a cinema that interrogates the founding violence behind the photograph of a state.

Theo Angelopoulos (b. 1935), the great elegist of Greek modernism whose slow-cinema grammar descends from Mizoguchi and Jancsó yet answers to no one, made The Travelling Players (O Thiasos) in 1975 as the colonels' junta was collapsing—a four-hour film shot partly in secret, dodging censors. Its symbolic geography stretches from the depopulated platforms of Aegion to the fog-bound squares of provincial Macedonia, places that dissolve into a single haunted national stage where time folds back on itself. At its center stands Electra, the troupe's keeper of memory, summoned straight from the House of Atreus yet stripped of catharsis—an Aeschylean avenger who inherits the curse but is denied the cleansing the myth once promised. The very title, with its itinerant 'thiasos' (the ancient term for a Dionysian theatrical band), asks whether a people condemned to perform the same pastoral forever can ever finish their own story, or merely wander between regimes reciting borrowed lines: who writes the script when history keeps interrupting the play? Advancing the European art-cinema of the long take into outright political archaeology, this is the foundational masterwork of Balkan slow cinema—essential viewing for anyone who believes form itself can carry the weight of a century.

Elio Petri (1929–1982), the Roman Marxist provocateur whose grotesque, lacquered satires fused Italian neorealist conscience with the icy formalism of European modernism, made this 1970 Oscar-winning film at the apex of a career devoted to anatomizing power. Set in a Rome of cold marble ministries and a bourgeois apartment turned crime-scene theatre, it converges the seat of state authority and the private chamber of desire into a single psychic prison. Its protagonist, a newly promoted chief of the political bureau played by Gian Maria Volonté, begins as a Dostoevskian Raskolnikov who has committed the perfect crime—but inverts him, demanding not absolution but accusation. The Italian title, Indagine su un cittadino al di sopra di ogni sospetto, lingers on that bureaucratic phrase 'above suspicion,' a juridical impossibility worn as armour: if the law cannot touch its own enforcers, what could the word 'guilt' even mean? Arriving amid Italy's anni di piombo and scored by Ennio Morricone's circus-like jeer, it remains the supreme achievement of the Italian political-grotesque cinema, weaponizing Brechtian distance and operatic excess to make the spectator complicit in the very impunity it dissects.

Jennifer Kent (b. 1969), an Australian actor-turned-auteur who studied under Lars von Trier on the set of Dogville, made her feature debut with a film that fused the disreputable machinery of the horror genre with the austere psychological gravity of post-war European art cinema. Set in a sunless suburban Adelaide house whose grey-blue interiors feel less like Australia than like a chamber of the unconscious — and a pop-up storybook whose pages open onto a second, papery dimension — the film converges domestic naturalism and Expressionist menace into a single suffocating space. Its protagonist, Amelia, a widowed nursing-home carer worn thin by grief, begins as the archetypal beleaguered mother of melodrama before mutating into something the maternal ideal forbids us to imagine. The title creature's stuttered, onomatopoeic name — 'Babadook' — sounds like a child's nonsense and a buried command at once: if it cannot be killed, what does it mean to live with what you cannot kill? Arriving amid the early-2010s 'elevated horror' wave alongside It Follows and The Witch, The Babadook advanced the maternal-Gothic tradition by making the monster not an invader but a tenant — and earned a place among the decade's defining genre works.

Luis Buñuel (b. 1900), the Aragonese surrealist who detonated cinema with Un Chien Andalou (1929) and spent a career flaying the Catholic bourgeoisie, made this 45-minute fragment as the coda to his Mexican exile, a miniature distilling the anticlerical venom of Viridiana (1961) and Nazarín (1959). Its world is built from two converging poles: the Syrian wilderness of 4th-century Christendom where the historical Simeon Stylites stood, and the Mexican desert outside Mexico City where Buñuel actually filmed — a barren plain that becomes a stage for the absurdity of grace. At its center stands Simon (Claudio Brook), an anchorite cast in the mold of the desert saint, the holy fool perched between earth and heaven, who quietly mutates into something stranger than sanctity. The Spanish title, Simón del desierto, fixes a man by his emptiness — desert as both地理 and spiritual condition: is the desert the place sanctity flees to, or the void it secretly is? A landmark of cinematic Surrealism and its blasphemous comedy, this unfinished masterpiece compresses Buñuel's lifelong assault on faith into one vertiginous gesture that still detonates.

Sergio Leone (b. 1929), the Roman architect of the Spaghetti Western who detonated Hollywood's myths from across the Atlantic, here completes his so-called Dollars Trilogy at the peak of his operatic, time-dilating style — extreme close-ups stretched against vast emptiness, Ennio Morricone's score composed before shooting so actors could move to it. Between the dust-choked battlefields of an American Civil War and the Spanish badlands of Almería and Burgos where they were conjured, the film opens a purgatorial space where geography dissolves into pure greed. Its nominal hero, the quiet bounty hunter Blondie (Clint Eastwood), descends from the laconic gunslinger lineage of Shane and Ringo, yet drains that archetype of all moral certainty until 'good' becomes merely a degree. The Italian title, 'Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo,' reorders the moral hierarchy the English title fixes — and asks: when survival is the only law, what separates the virtuous man from the ugly one but luck and a faster draw? As the keystone of the Spaghetti Western, it transformed a disreputable subgenre into mythic, ironic American epic — the film every revisionist Western since has had to answer.

Zhang Yimou (b. 1950), the Fifth Generation colourist who once drenched Raise the Red Lantern and Hero in saturated crimson and gold, here performs an audacious reversal, draining nearly all hue from the frame in the late, austere chapter of a career that helped define Chinese cinema's global ascent. The film's world coalesces from two opposing zones — the contested border town of Jingzhou and the rain-darkened palace court of Pei — fusing into a single grisaille battlefield where every wall, robe, and calligraphy screen dissolves into the wet silk of a Song-dynasty ink-wash painting. Its protagonist, the wounded commander Ziyu, presents himself first as the canonical wuxia strategist-warrior, yet quickly subverts that archetype by ruling through a body that is not his own. The Chinese title, 影 (Yǐng) — 'shadow,' the term for a body-double — points past mere disguise toward a Hwadu: if a man governs entirely through his copy, where does the self reside, and which one casts the other? Advancing the wuxia film beyond the airborne spectacle of its 2000s heyday into a chamber-scaled meditation on duplicity, Shadow proves the genre can turn inward without surrendering its choreography.

Scott Derrickson (b. 1966), the Denver-bred genre stylist who fused Catholic dread with multiplex horror in Sinister (2012) and The Exorcism of Emily Rose (2005) before a detour through Marvel's Doctor Strange, returns to his hometown and to the Joe Hill source story that suits his sensibility better than any blockbuster could. Late-1970s Denver becomes a symbolic terrain where suburban wood-paneled normalcy and a windowless soundproof basement converge into a single psychic geography of childhood — the surface world of bullies and absent fathers atop a buried chamber of the disappeared. At its center is Finney Blake, a passive, bullied thirteen-year-old cast initially as the helpless prey of the slasher's final-girl lineage, only to transcend that archetype by inheriting strength from the dead. The title's severed instrument — a black phone that should carry nothing — rings anyway, posing its lingering Hwadu: what do the silenced owe the living, and can a voice survive the body that spoke it? Advancing the late-period American 'elevated horror' wave alongside It Follows and The Babadook, while reviving the Stephen-King-adjacent 'kid in peril' tradition of Stand By Me and It, The Black Phone proves that supernatural terror can be, at heart, a study of inheritance.

Wu Yonggang (b. 1907), a designer-turned-director whose debut announced one of the most controlled visual sensibilities of the late silent era, fashioned in The Goddess a film that distilled the social-realist current of Shanghai's Lianhua Film Company into pure pictorial economy. Its world hangs between two converging spaces: the glowing streetlamp of the nocturnal pavement and the bare schoolroom of a respectable daylight city, the demimonde and the bourgeois institution pressing against one another along a single brick wall. Its protagonist, the unnamed mother played by Ruan Lingyu, arrives looking like the fallen woman of melodrama—the Magdalene of countless silents—only to dismantle that archetype through a stillness and interiority no title card could supply. The Chinese title 神女 (shénnǚ), at once 'goddess' and a period euphemism for a streetwalker, holds the film's whole argument in two characters: how can one word name both the sacred and the despised? Made on the eve of Chinese sound cinema and the leftist film boom of the 1930s, this is the silent melodrama at its most rigorous and humane—evidence of how much a face, held long enough, can say.

Celine Song (b. 1988), the Korean-Canadian playwright-turned-filmmaker who arrived with the Oscar-nominated Past Lives (2023) and its bruising grammar of restraint, returns with a second feature that converts romance into ledger. Her terrain is a New York suspended between the glass towers of the Financial District and the thin-walled walk-ups of the outer boroughs, two skylines that become a moral topography of who one is allowed to love. At its center stands Lucy, a professional matchmaker — a figure descended from Austen's Emma and the screwball intermediary, but stripped of whimsy and re-tooled as an asset manager of the heart. The title Materialists names not greed but a philosophy: the conviction that persons are quantities, that desire can be priced. Yet the word haunts itself — what, exactly, is the matter of a human being, and can love survive being weighed? Working in the recent vein of the prestige anti-romcom, Song advances a movement that turns the romantic comedy against its own utopias, drawing on her theatrical instinct for two people talking in a room until the air changes. This is a film about commerce that refuses to be transactional with its audience.

Zhang Yimou (b. 1950), the cinematographer-turned-director whose Fifth Generation lyricism made saturated colour an instrument of social critique, here refines the painterly mode of Red Sorghum (1987) into something colder and more architectural. The film converges two symbolic spaces: the grey, walled Chen family compound of northern Shanxi and the Qiao family courtyards of Pingyao where it was shot — a feudal labyrinth that becomes a psychological prison of corridors, rooftops, and rigid frontal symmetry. Its protagonist, Songlian, the nineteen-year-old educated girl who arrives as fourth mistress, recalls the tragic ingénue of classical melodrama only to dismantle that archetype, learning that intelligence is no defence against ritual. The original title, Da Hong Denglong Gao Gao Gua (大紅燈籠高高掛) — 'big red lanterns hung high' — frames celebration and seduction as instruments of surveillance, and leaves a Hwadu suspended in the cold air: when the light that marks your worth can be hooded at another's whim, who is truly chosen and who is merely lit? As a landmark of post-1989 Chinese art cinema, it advances the Fifth Generation's allegorical project, turning national costume drama into a forensic anatomy of power.

Satyajit Ray (b. 1921), the Bengali humanist whose Apu Trilogy redefined Indian cinema's place in the world, here turns from the village lyricism of his early work to the granular sociology of urban modernity, joining the line of realists who watched ordinary lives bend under economic strain. The film converges two symbolic geographies: the swarming trams, offices and stairwells of a 1950s–60s Calcutta hungry for white-collar wages, and the single cramped middle-class flat where three generations breathe each other's air. Its protagonist, Arati, a housewife turned door-to-door saleswoman, begins as the dutiful Bengali wife of legend and quietly becomes something the archetype was never meant to contain.
